title: Quantum computational advantage in random-circuit sampling on IBM superconducting quantum computers
authors: Tigran Sedrakyan, Yuxuan Zhang, Hovnatan Karapetyan, Joshua D. Baktay, Hrant Gharibyan, Hayk Tepanyan
abstract: We report forward random-circuit sampling (RCS) on the 120-qubit Nighthawk r2 superconducting processor (\textit{ibm\_phoenix}) with square-lattice connectivity, using 61 qubits, native CZ gates, and the standard cloud execution stack with no benchmark-specific calibration. Two independent fidelity estimators---mirror benchmarking and three- and four-patch cross-entropy benchmarking (XEB)---agree with each other at every measured depth, the mirror from 4 to 40 cycles and the patched estimators from 20 to 40 cycles, across more than two orders of magnitude of fidelity decay, and exceed the first-generation Nighthawk r1 device by more than an order of magnitude at fixed depth. The 36-cycle circuits sit at the depth where tensor-network contraction cost saturates at system size: a contraction-cost estimator validated against the published Sycamore and Zuchongzhi networks places the single-amplitude cost at $\sim$$10^{22}$ complex operations. At $F_{\mathrm{XEB}}(36)=2.3\times10^{-3}$ under favorable memory assumptions this implies $1.2\times10^{27}$ machine operations within the bounded-fidelity rejection-sampling model --- more than a century of runtime on the Frontier supercomputer --- to collect a $10^{6}$-sample ensemble, which takes only 19\,s on Nighthawk r2. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of quantum advantage for a vanilla random-circuit sampling on a commercially and broadly accessible quantum processor that most non-expert quantum computer users can easily replicate.
summary: This work demonstrates quantum computational advantage by executing random-circuit sampling on a superconducting quantum processor. The authors rigorously benchmarked the device's fidelity using multiple estimators and calculated the classical resources needed to simulate the results. This comparison shows that the quantum hardware can achieve the required computation in seconds, whereas classical supercomputers would require centuries.
main_problem: The paper aims to demonstrate quantum computational advantage by performing random-circuit sampling (RCS) on a commercially available superconducting quantum processor.
main_result: They report the first demonstration of quantum advantage for vanilla RCS on such a processor, showing that the required classical simulation time vastly exceeds the runtime on the Nighthawk r2 device.
method: The authors used multiple fidelity estimators (mirror and XEB) to characterize the performance of the superconducting quantum processor across varying circuit depths.
model_or_system: The experiment utilizes a 120-qubit superconducting quantum processor (Nighthawk r2) with square-lattice connectivity, implementing RCS using 61 qubits and native CZ gates.
key_observables: Circuit fidelity (measured by mirror and XEB estimators), computational cost estimates (in complex operations), and runtime comparison against classical supercomputers.
important_parameters: Circuit depth (up to 40 cycles), fidelity decay rates, and the required number of samples ($10^6$).
main_assumptions: The classical cost estimate relies on the bounded-fidelity rejection-sampling model and assumes favorable memory conditions for the simulation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate error maps, the selected qubit connectivity, and the randomized patching methodology used for fidelity estimation across circuit depths.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by benchmarking fidelity using multiple estimators, quantifying the computational cost required for classical simulation at a fixed depth, and finally comparing this cost to the achievable runtime on the quantum hardware.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete, hardware-validated demonstration of quantum advantage using a method (RCS) that is highly relevant to understanding the scaling limits of near-term quantum computation.
